Rafael, before we plan month two, I have a concern. My team's workload is too high.
I see. What is your capacity this month?
About eighty percent. Two of my engineers have to be on call every night, so they are tired.
Then they don't have to do every night. Let's share the nights with my team.
That helps a lot. And do we have to send the long report every week?
No, you don't have to. A short update on Friday is enough. But you mustn't change production without telling us.
Fair. What about the manual access report? We don't have the bandwidth for it now.
I'll delegate it to Marcos on my team. He has to automate it by the end of May.

I lead a support team of eight people, and my most important job is to protect their capacity. When the workload is too high, people work overtime, and after a month they start to make mistakes. So we have three simple rules. First, nobody has to be on call two weeks in a row. We change every Monday. Second, our weekly meeting is optional for anyone with nothing new to say. You don't have to come; you just have to write two lines in the chat. Third, and this one is mandatory: you mustn't say yes to a new request without checking your bandwidth first. A tired team doesn't need more meetings. It needs fewer tasks and clear limits.

For years, I had a problem: I didn't know how to delegate. I used to think that a good manager has to know everything and do the difficult tasks himself. So I worked overtime almost every night, and my team waited for me. Then my director asked me a simple question: which tasks do you really have to do yourself? The honest answer was: very few. I made a list. Approving the budget, talking to the board and hiring are mine. Everything else, I don't have to do. Now each engineer owns one area, and I only check the results on Friday. My team is faster, and I go home at six. The lesson was clear: if you never delegate, you become the bottleneck.
